For, as the author says, “Every discussion of a subject undertaken rationally ought to begin with a definition, so that what is being discussed may be understood” (Cicero, On Duties 1.7). Thus, just as we discussed the definitions of justice and sin above, let us now consider what definition belongs to freedom of choice, so that it may be clear which of us agrees with it and which opposes it. Freedom of choice, by which God gave the human being independence, consists in the capacity to commit sin and to abstain from sin.

For the human being was made a rational, mortal living being, capable of virtue and vice. Through the capacity granted to him, he could either keep God's commands or transgress them, or by nature's teaching preserve the law of human fellowship. He was free to will either alternative; in this lies the substance of sin and justice. For when he draws something according to virtue for those in need, either from the springs of mercy or from the breasts of justice, it is justice itself working outwardly, which a holy will conceived and brought forth within.

Likewise, on the opposite side, when someone resolves to act wrongly to others' injury and becomes unjust or cruel, the act by which he harms others comes outward from the wickedness that an evil will sowed and generated within. But when the means are lacking by which the force of the hidden will may break out against one's neighbors, the character of kindness or malice is nevertheless complete in that will alone, when it has accomplished something good or evil not through a brief impulse but through deliberate thought and desire.
The capacity for good and the capacity for evil are therefore both good. Being able to do good is the palace of virtue; being able to do evil is the testimony of freedom.

A person can therefore possess a good that is his own precisely because he also has the capacity to do evil. The entire fullness of divine judgment is so closely bound up with this human freedom that whoever recognizes one knows both. Consequently, whoever violates one violates both. Let the freedom of human choice therefore be preserved just as divine fairness is preserved. This is the understanding of free choice that has subjected belief in fate, the calculations of Chaldean astrologers, and the fantasies of the Manichaeans to the Church's truth. This is the understanding that shows you too, along with those we have listed, to be strangers to Christ. Freedom of choice, then, is the capacity either to commit or to avoid sin, free from compelling necessity. It has within its own authority which of the alternatives that arise it follows: either the steep and rugged heights of the virtues or the sunken marshes of pleasures.

To state it briefly, it is a capacity whose sole watchful task is to ensure that no one is either driven into sin or dragged away from sin by someone else while the will is held captive. That the will cannot be captured unless it chooses to surrender is shown by courage, whose strength in despising pain has constantly shone forth among both pagans and Christians.

If, then, as reason has disclosed, freedom of choice excludes compulsion, so that no one is either good or evil without being free to be the opposite, how could you acknowledge free choice while about to use a testimony suited to captives? Or how could you append such a testimony after acknowledging free choice? You say: “We do not deny free choice. But Truth says, ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free’” (John 8:36). It is clear that in that passage Christ addressed a captive conscience. He showed it to be not free, but subject to the punishment that condemns sins committed by free will. You misunderstand that statement, that is, you do not understand it, or perhaps you understand it as applying to yourself, but drag it here against its own nature. You have put it in a place where its whole proper meaning conflicts with your words. Let us join the words themselves: what is set free is captive; what is captive is not free; what is free is not captive.

Simply acknowledge whichever of these you choose, then, and stop quibbling. Either say with us that choice is free, and remove the testimony that was appropriately spoken in its own setting, or say, as in those books you have now sent to Boniface through Alypius, that the choice we call free is captive, and stop denying that you are a Manichaean.

These two things you join together, free and not free, that is, free and captive, cannot both fit the thing under discussion. But they testify that you possess extraordinary foolishness, a new shamelessness, and an old impiety.

It is now time to discuss the Gospel's statement. The evangelist John says: “Jesus said to the Jews who had believed in him, ‘If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free’” (John 8:31–32). That is, our Lord Jesus was telling those who believed in him not to rejoice in worldly nobility or claim glory from Abraham's descent, but to strive and labor for virtue and, after recognizing Christ, to serve no sins. They would thereby retain true freedom with a joyful conscience and, through hope in things that are certain, that is, eternal, be freed from desire for everything else, which because of its fragility is frequently called empty and false.

Then the Jews, not understanding what freedom Jesus meant, answered him: “We are Abraham's offspring and have never been anyone's slaves. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?” (John 8:33). “Freedom” is commonly used in many senses. Here it means holiness. In the apostle it means resurrection, when he says that creation is to be freed from slavery to corruption into the glorious freedom of God's children (Romans 8:21). In its better-known sense it is spoken of in contrast to slavery. The same name is also used for freedom of choice. Let us therefore distinguish the cases, so that things far apart are not confused because they share a name. Here the Lord does not say that freedom of choice needs to be set free. Rather, while it remains intact, he calls on the Jews to receive forgiveness and be freed from guilt, obtaining the freedom that is greatest in God's sight: to begin to owe no debt for crimes.

The evangelist continues: “Jesus answered them, ‘Amen, amen, I tell you: everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. If, then, the Son sets you free, you will be truly free’” (John 8:34–36).

He made plain the slavery of which he was speaking: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). How forcefully this very statement opposes your error! He says that no one is a slave of sin except someone who has himself committed sin, and that sin cannot cling to anyone unless the person in question has personally committed it, either in action or even by will alone. How clearly he also shows that the whole human race cannot now be possessed by the devil, when he distinguishes between slave and son, that is, between the just and the unjust! Here Christ separated not only himself but each of the saints from the condition of slaves. Such people existed both before and during the Old Testament; he declares that they remain in his Father's house and rejoice at his table (Luke 13:28–29). This whole kind of exhortation would have been pointlessly spoken if he were not addressing people with free choice.

To make you understand that he reproaches their lives rather than their nature, he continues: “I know that you are Abraham's children” (John 8:37). There is the dignity of descent on account of which they had declared themselves free. Now he shows the slavery to which they are subject: “You seek to kill me, because my word finds no room in you. I speak what I have heard with my Father; and you do what you have seen with your father” (John 8:37–38).

See how different the accounts of nature and will are. Jesus did not deny that their flesh belonged to Abraham's offspring. But he presses upon them that through an unjust will they had moved to the devil as their father, who is called their begetter because he is shown to be their teacher in crimes. “The Jews answered and said to him, ‘Abraham is our father.’ Jesus said to them, ‘If you were Abraham's children, you would do Abraham's works. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth I heard from God. Abraham did not do this; you do the works of your father’” (John 8:39–41). Do you see the distinctions Wisdom makes in its language? He denies that they are Abraham's children after saying above that they were Abraham's children. But because nature and will require different treatment, he shows that the ancestor of their innocent flesh is one person, and the deceiver of their wretched will another.

Here, then, when the Lord said, “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John 8:36), he promised forgiveness to guilty people who, by sinning, had lost not freedom of choice but a righteous conscience. Free choice remains as complete after sins as it was before sins. Indeed, it is through its action that many renounce the hidden things of shame and, casting away the filth of disgraceful deeds, clothe themselves in the distinctions of virtue (2 Corinthians 4:2).

Stop making yourself impious, then, if any distinction between right and wrong still remains for you, by explaining Christ's words as though he had denied free choice. Without that choice remaining intact, the fairness of his own judgment cannot stand.

Listen to where he shows the power of human freedom: “I came in my Father's name, and you did not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him” (John 5:43). And again: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matthew 12:33). And again: “If you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works” (John 10:38). Most forcefully of all, he says that his intention was hindered by human will: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matthew 23:37). He does not then add, “But I gathered you against your will.” Rather: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:38). Thus he shows that they are rightly punished for their evil action, but ought not to have been forced away from their own intention by any compulsion. In the same way he had spoken through the prophet: “If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land. If you are unwilling and do not listen, the sword will devour you” (Isaiah 1:19–20). How, then, do you not deny free choice, when you pronounced it unfree, not indeed in your own wording but through the Gospel's testimony as interpreted by you?

In the work which I said above you recently sent to Rome, you revealed your meaning more boldly. In its first book, having similarly set before yourself our charge that you deny free choice, you argue as follows, you most consistent and subtle debater: “Which of us says that through the first human being's sin free choice perished from the human race? Freedom indeed perished through sin, but the freedom that existed in paradise to possess complete righteousness with immortality. Human nature therefore needs divine grace, as the Lord says in his Gospel: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free’ (John 8:36), that is, free to live well and justly. Free choice has so far not perished in the sinner that through it people sin, especially all who sin with pleasure and love of sin and approve what they enjoy. Hence the apostle says: ‘When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness’ (Romans 6:20). See, they are shown to have been unable even to serve sin except by another sort of freedom. They are free from righteousness only by freedom of choice, but are freed from sin only by the Savior's grace. For this reason that admirable teacher carefully distinguished even the words: ‘When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit did you then have in the things of which you are now ashamed? Their end is death. But now, freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have your fruit leading to sanctification and your end eternal life’ (Romans 6:20–22). He called them free from righteousness, not freed from it. But regarding sin he very carefully preferred to call them not free, lest they attribute this to themselves, but freed, referring this to the Lord's statement: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free.’ Since the children of humanity do not live well unless they become God's children, why does this man want to attribute the power of living well to free choice? This power is given only by ‘God's grace through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Romans 7:25), as the Gospel says: ‘To as many as received him he gave power to become God's children’” (John 1:12; Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.2.4) (Genesis 1:26–27).

A little later you say again: “The power is therefore given to those who believe in him to become God's children. Unless God gives this power, none can come from free choice. For what the liberator has not freed will not be free for good. But a person has choice free for evil when a hidden or open deceiver has implanted delight in wickedness, or when that person has persuaded himself to it. Thus it is not the case, as some say we claim and as this man even dares to write, that everyone is forced into sin against his will, as it were, by the necessity of his flesh. Rather, if people are old enough to exercise the choice of their own mind, they are held in sin by their own will and plunge from sin into sin by their own will. But this will, free in evil because it delights in evil, is not free in good because it has not been freed. A human being cannot will anything good unless helped by the one who cannot will evil” (Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.6–7).

In all these words of yours that I have quoted, I see grace's name so entangled with denial of free choice that the goodness of the names cannot vindicate the evil of your meaning. Rather, the dignity of the names is degraded by attachment to your doctrines. You have not made yourself honorable by these words; you have dishonored the ornaments themselves. We, however, separate what you have joined, so that the divinity of grace, disentangled from these perverse connections, will suffer no attack from our reply and will be praised with catholic seriousness rather than Manichaean flattery.

We therefore acknowledge Christ's grace in its many forms. Its first gift is that we were made from nothing. Its second is that, just as through sensation we surpass things that merely live, so through reason we surpass things that sense. Reason was impressed upon the mind to disclose the Creator's image; the granted freedom of choice belongs equally to that dignity (compare Genesis 1:26–27). To this same grace we credit the increase of benefits he never ceases to bestow on us. This grace sent the Law as a help (Isaiah 8:20, LXX wording). Its task was to awaken by many kinds of teaching, and nourish by its invitation, the light of reason that examples of wrongdoing and habitual vices were dimming. To the fullness of this grace, that is, the divine goodwill that gave things their existence, belonged the Word's becoming flesh and dwelling among us (John 1:14). For God, asking his image to return his love, made clear with what immeasurable affection he had done everything for us. Thus we might, even if late, love in return the one who, commending his love toward us (Romans 5:8), did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us (Romans 8:32), promising that if we henceforth chose to obey his will, he would make us fellow heirs with his Only Begotten (Romans 8:17).

added_allusions.reason: Reason and freedom disclose the Creator’s image.

translator_notes: “The Law as a help” follows the source’s reference to the LXX form of Isaiah 8:20, whose wording differs from familiar modern translations. Augustine’s argument about “free” and “freed” is retained because the distinction itself is being contested.

english: This grace, then, which in baptism not only forgives sins but along with that gift of pardon also advances, adopts, and consecrates us, changes what the guilty deserve. It does not create free choice, which we receive when we are created and use when we acquire the power to distinguish good and evil. We therefore do not deny that countless forms of divine help assist a good will. But this does not mean that these forms of help construct a freedom of choice that had been destroyed, or that at some time freedom is excluded and a necessity of either good or evil is thought to lie upon anyone. Rather, every help cooperates with free choice.

It is solely because of this free choice, the Teacher of the Nations writes, that we must be revealed before Christ's judgment seat, so that each may receive what belongs to the body's deeds, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5:10). Catholics acknowledge this free choice, but you deny it, not only with Mani but also with Jovinian, whom you dare to pin on us. Your denial takes a different form but involves similar impiety. To make this clearer, let us examine the distinctions. We say that a person's sin changes not the state of nature but the character of what the person deserves. That is, in the sinner the nature of free choice remains the same: through it he can cease from sin, just as through it he was able to depart from righteousness.

The Manichaean says that an evil will is inspired by a nature that cannot will good, while a good will is poured in by a nature that cannot will evil. Thus he imposes on the natures of each kind of thing a necessity such that their own wills cannot will the opposite. There is certainly a great gulf between him and us. Let us now see how far you have departed from him. You say that the will is free, but only to do evil; it is not free to cease doing evil unless a necessity of willing good is imposed on it by that nature which, to use your words, “cannot will evil” (Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.7). You therefore define the human race as doing nothing through free choice except sinning, and as unable to do anything else. By this you declare outright that human nature always desires only one thing, evil, and cannot will the opposite. God's nature, however, cannot will evil; therefore, unless it makes evil human nature share in its own necessity, no good action can exist in human nature. After this, God may see in the secrecy of your heart whether you have little love for Mani. But as far as the kinship of your doctrines shows, you have done absolutely nothing except change the order and establish the same thing he asserted.

You are joined to Jovinian on one point. In the second book of his work he says that a baptized person cannot sin, while before baptism a person can both sin and refrain from sin. With you, then, he thinks that from the time of baptism a necessity of good is imposed on human beings. This is just as false as your belief that before baptism human beings possess a necessity of doing evil. For when you say, “A human being cannot will anything good unless helped by the one who cannot will evil” (Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.7), you mean that through sharing in grace and a good nature a person obtains the capacity to do good; you say, however, that this can happen from the time of baptism. Caught between impiety and fear, you have therefore fled to Jovinian's company, but have not yet left Mani's brothel. Yet Jovinian is as much more innocent than you as Mani is more profane than Jovinian.

To gather up our argument still more briefly: the Manichaean says, “In all human beings the nature of darkness, which inspires the evil will, sins and cannot do anything else.” You say, “In all human beings nature, infected by the darkness of the first sin and therefore the author of an evil will, sins and cannot will good.” Jovinian says, “The human will does indeed sin, but only up to baptism; afterward it can will nothing but good.” Catholics, that is, we, say that from beginning to end there is no compulsion from anything belonging to nature. In each person it is the will that sins, including before baptism; at the very time it sins it has the power to depart from evil and do good, so that freedom remains a reality.

None of you therefore possesses true doctrine. Nevertheless, since you set out from a single starting point of error, it would at least have been less dishonorable to accept the consequences. Since you say with Mani that sin occurs through an evil nature, that is, through defective freedom, you should also have said with him that it cannot be cleansed in any way. You do affirm this elsewhere; but you should have added its necessary consequence, that it therefore has no need of baptism's sacraments. Or if you assert with Jovinian that good desires are imprinted from the time faith is received, you should have said with him that nature was good even before baptism: although it had the capacity for evil, it did not have its necessity, and so by consecration it reached an unmistakable good. In this way, even if you opposed reason, at least you would not contradict the doctrines of those you follow.
As it is, however, faithless to everyone, you say that a necessity of sin has arisen in the nature of the flesh,

so that, having lost the possession of eternity, which it plainly never possessed by its origin, the will would be bent continually upon seeking wrongdoing. And you add: “The will that is free in evil is not free in good.” With a declaration of foolishness no less than of profanity, you call something free while saying it can will only one thing.

Although you are consistent in no respect, let the sensible reader consider what you have advanced. Let us agree that a will unable to will good can be called free. You assert that this will is freed in baptism. I ask: in what way is it freed? Is it compelled always to will good and unable to will evil? Or can it desire either? If you answer, “It is compelled always to will good”, you yourself recognize how much of a Jovinianist you are. If, however, you say, “How can a will be free if it is compelled always to will good?”, I answer, “How was it called free before, if it was compelled to will only evil?” If you therefore reply that after baptism the will becomes free in the sense that it can both sin and refrain from sin, you thereby declare that there was no free choice when it could not do both. You are enclosed on every side by the snares of your own argument. If choice was free before baptism, it had the capacity to do good just as it had the capacity to do evil; and the whole stage set of your doctrine, by which you urge an evil inherent in nature, collapses.

But if it was not free for good before, and after baptism became free in the sense that it could not do evil, then it never possessed freedom of choice. It is shown to have sinned without guilt before and afterward to possess the glory of holiness without effort.

Once this is established, you are proved to deny your own doctrine outright when you promise that you do not deny free choice, which you overthrow first by the necessity of evil and afterward by the necessity of good.

Recalling our earlier definitions, however, also helps demolish your doctrine completely. If sin is nothing but the will to retain and commit what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain, then on your account no sin can be found anywhere in reality.
translator_notes: “On your account” makes explicit that Julian is drawing a consequence from Augustine’s position, not denying that sin exists.

english: For if justice imputes only what one is free to abstain from, and before baptism there is a necessity of evil, since the will, as you said, is not free to do good and consequently can do nothing but evil, then the very necessity it suffers defends it against the disgrace of evil. It cannot be burdened with its deeds before that justice which imputes no evil except what one is free to abstain from. After baptism, however, if there is a necessity of good, there certainly cannot be any sin. See, then, how impossible it is to find in seed what reason shows sin to be, when according to your definitions it can no longer be found even in conduct.

With this conclusion of our discussion sealed in the sensible reader's mind, let us examine how your baptism, which you say was provided solely because of the stirring of the genitals, performs its entrusted task. It professes to cleanse human beings from sins. But when the will's case is heard before justice, a will that could not will otherwise is not pronounced guilty. When the accusation of guilt vanishes, the display of pardon vanishes too: one cannot forgive what one cannot rightly impute. Thus it fails to fulfill its promise. It finds no crimes whose forgiveness might earn it praise, nor anyone indebted to it for the benefit by which the bonds of sins are loosed, because it cannot convict those sheltered in the sanctuary of necessity of an evil will. All this shows it to be superfluous.

But the grace provided by Christ is not superfluous. Let us retain a rational account of its generosity, by which the sinner's will is proved guilty, since it could certainly have willed good just as it willed evil. The entire fiction of necessity therefore vanishes. Consequently, there is no sin from the condition of nature; free choice remains in human nature. You deny it with the Manichaeans; we acknowledge it with the apostles and all catholics.

Your explanation of the apostle Paul's words would deserve to be passed over with a laugh if it did not frighten those unfamiliar with Scripture. The apostle says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Romans 6:20). He certainly could not have said “freed”. The language of liberation is fittingly and properly used when a person is freed from harmful things. Those who resolve to owe nothing to the virtues, however, can be called free from virtues. A person can therefore be called free either from good or from evil when, serving one, he aims to owe nothing to the other. But a person can be called freed only from evil, because the word “liberation” contains a sign of the distress that is driven away. What difficulty, then, could be raised here about the apostle's words when, following ordinary human usage, he called them free from good and freed from evil?

He says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6:20–21). But lest you suppose that we become slaves of sin through nature, hear the apostle himself speaking in the same passage: “Do you not know that when you present yourselves as slaves to obey someone, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin or of obedience to righteousness?” (Romans 6:16). He says that you presented yourselves as slaves to sin, so that you would understand him to impute sin to will, not birth. He therefore called them free from righteousness solely because they had refused to keep its commands.

He immediately adds that they are slaves of righteousness in the same way that they had previously been slaves of sin. You may now, if you wish, call them free from sin when they serve righteousness, just as he called them free from righteousness when they served wrongdoing. Most foolishly, then, you wanted to bring an accusation against the apostle's straightforward language. He did not, as you think, very carefully indicate the point you imagine; rather, you are very sleepily examining what he said. You argue that he preferred to say “freed” rather than “free” so that we would understand that freedom of choice enables evil but cannot bring about good. Yet the very order of his words resists you. If he had thought as you do, that freedom produced only sin, he should have said, “You were free for sin”, not “You were free for righteousness” (Romans 6:20), so that a person would be called free with respect to what that freedom accomplished. If we are to weigh even the force of grammatical cases, he said that they were free “for this righteousness”, not free “from this righteousness”. His phrasing would therefore help us more consistently, if we too wished to press such slight matters. Far be it from us! We understand the apostle's meaning and are content with the service of words straightforwardly spoken.

The Teacher of the Nations meant nothing other than: “You were free; you did not serve righteousness. You have been freed; you have received forgiveness of sins.” Freedom of choice remains, through which they could obey sin before and righteousness afterward.

english: He shows what his exhortation contains by saying first: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you presented your members to serve impurity and lawlessness leading to lawlessness, so now present your members to serve righteousness leading to sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Romans 6:19–20). With perfect consistency he says that those whom he had urged to keep their members in complete sanctification had been free from righteousness.

We have spent no little time here proving the complete certainty of what I said earlier in section 73: people terrified by your speech would deny free choice and be driven by empty fear into real destruction; and you are the chief denier of free choice. Let us therefore return to the book addressed to Valerius, to prove that at first you denied God as Creator, while now you deny him in some places and in others acknowledge him far more wickedly than you denied him. How absolutely you denied God as humanity's Creator in that earlier book of yours became sufficiently clear when it was examined. You said that the devil rightly plucked the human race like the fruit of a shrub he himself had planted (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 1.26). You added many other things, offered as arguments, that support this error. In this second book, although your doctrine as a whole pursues the same course, you attempt to amend your former statement in a more destructive way.

Let us briefly complete, however, the reply owed to the passage of yours quoted above in section 74. I answer firmly and faithfully that we do not begrudge human beings their liberator, the Lord Jesus Christ. We urge them not to believe you and be crushed by despair of amendment, abandoning Christ's teaching as though he commanded things that mortal nature could not grasp because it was burdened by an inborn evil.

Rather, let them run to the one who cries: “My yoke is gentle and my burden light” (Matthew 11:30). With immeasurable generosity he both grants pardon to an evil will and, through renewal and adoption, makes better the innocence that he creates good.

I therefore wonder that you dared to quote the testimony: “Whatever has overcome someone has made him its slave” (2 Peter 2:19). This most plainly supports us, who maintain that no one can be subject to the devil except someone who, after a contest of will, has been overcome by a base surrender. You should not have appropriated it, since it strongly opposes your attempt to persuade us that newborn children belong to the devil's kingdom. Without a will of their own, they could neither have been defeated nor have sinned.

Seeing that this weighs heavily against you, you act as though the testimony itself had asked: “How, then, are infants in the kingdom of the hostile power, if we believe Scripture that each person becomes the victor's slave when he is defeated, and if infancy, without the use of reason and will, plainly could neither fight nor surrender?” (Psalm 101:1;) You add: “For through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12). You continue: “God is the Creator of newborn children in such a way that all go from the one into condemnation unless he becomes their liberator through rebirth. For he is called ‘the potter making from the same lump one vessel for honor according to mercy, another for dishonor according to judgment’ (Romans 9:21), to whom the Church sings, ‘Mercy and judgment’” (Psalm 101:1; LXX Psalm 100:1; Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.8).

As for your statement that sin entered through one human being, the apostolic testimony by which you have stirred many hearts, though uneducated ones, I briefly showed in my fourth book how it should be understood. Yet with Christ's help we will explain it more fully in this work. In the second book we will set other things aside and discuss that apostolic passage most fully in its own context (see below, Book II, section 20).

english: Here I would briefly warn that it cannot support you in establishing an opinion which all learning, all reason, and God's Law convict of being utterly unjust. Let the attentive reader therefore notice your declaration that God is the maker of evil people, and creates people of such a kind that, without anything deserved by a will of their own, absolutely all of them go into condemnation.

So that we could not miss the period you mean, you declare that from Adam, who you say was all people in one, until the end, those who have not been baptized are found liable to condemnation and subject to the devil. By this opinion you try to cure yourself far more destructively than you previously wounded yourself. For to remove the hostility rushing upon you because you called the devil humanity's Creator, you correct yourself by acknowledging God as Creator, but of the sort of people the Manichaean assigns to the prince of darkness.

Believing human beings evil by the condition of birth, the Manichaean assigned them an author through whom the blame for the evil work could be kept away from the good God. Since he had erred in the definition of sin, thinking natural something that can only be voluntary, he consistently went on to invent an evil maker for an evil origin. In this he was more reverent toward God and more defiant toward nature. You, however, say that people are born evil, but that God is the author of the evil: you are more defiant toward God and more respectful toward nature. For nature is defended by its author's majesty, while its author is accused by the ugliness of his work.

You did not fear, most wicked man, to apply to God something for which the Manichaean invented another creator precisely to avoid attributing it to him. Both of you are enemies of the truth, but before you it was thought impossible to surpass him in impiety.

You, however, have “justified your sister Sodom”, as the prophet says (Ezekiel 16:48, 51, 55). The Manichaean will seem acquitted if compared with your blasphemies. In the first book of my work I had boasted that I was attacked by the mouth from which the apostles too had suffered injury. Now I am awed by the greatness of my good fortune: I am reviled by someone who brings charges against God.

How did I come to deserve the dignity of so great an insult? By praising me you could have bestowed nothing like it. You say my views deserve rejection, but God's works deserve condemnation. You declare that I argue badly, but that God creates wickedly. You shout that I err, but that he is cruel. You assert that I do not know the Law, but that God does not know justice. You cry out that I am not catholic because I say Christ calls people in order to save them; but you swear that God creates people to condemn them, and brings them into being for no other reason than that all should go into condemnation (compare Romans 5:18) (Romans 5:18).

english: I therefore see a great distance produced by the progress of your learning between you and Mani, the progenitor of your ideas. Although he introduced two authors, he left hope of salvation on the side on which he said that the good God was utterly removed from injustice and cruelty. You, however, by speaking of one good God who is also the Creator of evil people, have utterly abolished both reverence for divinity and hope of salvation.
For no one remains to help the guilty when the one who alone is God, from a desire to create misery, punishes even those in whom he recognizes nothing except what he himself made.

Having surveyed the abyss of your impiety, though nothing more profane could ever be found, a brief discussion will nevertheless show how powerless it is and what follows from the things you added. God, who wished to be called by this name, is believed to be supremely just as well as supremely powerful. If one of these is absent, neither will be present. He is humanity's most kindly Creator and the most equitable assessor of what each deserves. Everything he makes is very good (Genesis 1:31). Consequently, no one is evil by nature; whoever is guilty is accused for conduct, not origins.

Evil is therefore not inherent in nature, and God cannot create guilty people or place them in the devil's kingdom. These conclusions show you to be a Manichaean, indeed worse than a Manichaean. They also make clear that humanity enters this world without sin, that the fruit of human fertility is under God's authority rather than the devil's, and that nature is innocent.

With this established, consider what follows from your course of argument. The prophets and patriarchs and all the saints of the Old Testament plainly did not receive baptism, yet were created by God and afterward shone with their own virtues. They must therefore, against the Law's testimony, be believed to belong to the devil's kingdom and be destined for eternal punishments, because you declare that all are created from Adam for condemnation (compare Romans 5:18) (Romans 5:18).

english: If you say this, even your patrons will be able to acknowledge how openly Manichaean you are. But if you recognize so great an army of the true King fighting against your opinion, and realize that you cannot harm their standing, admit that what you built has been destroyed. Consequently, not everyone goes from one into condemnation (Romans 5:16), but only those who, rebellious against God's will, are overtaken by their final end without repentance or correction.

You should never have mentioned that God is called “the potter making from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor” (Romans 9:21). For as we explain it consistently, it wholly opposes you. When some are said to be made for honor and others for dishonor, this supports the catholic understanding that the different outcomes of the vessels correspond to the differences in human will.
But you, who had said above that everyone goes into condemnation, with what effrontery did you quote a testimony declaring that one goes to honor and another to dishonor?

Nothing is more contradictory than saying “all” (Romans 9:21) and “not all”. You say that God the potter makes everyone for condemnation. The apostle says that not everyone is for condemnation and not everyone for honor. I will explain the worth of this statement in its proper place. Even in the wording of the statement, however, there is plainly a great disagreement between you. The potter who shapes everyone for condemnation is not the same as the one Paul says fashions some for honor. You do not believe in the one proclaimed by that admirable teacher, because your potter shapes everyone for condemnation, while the apostle's potter shapes very many for glory (compare Romans 9:21).

english: I have said this to make it immediately apparent that you possess extraordinary ignorance or shamelessness, using statements opposed to you as though they were your own. Piety and reason, however, will explain that my God forms no one for dishonor,

but creates his image, that is, all human beings, good (compare Genesis 1:26–27). Even when they have been ruined by perverse pursuits, he desires to restore them through the generosity of his remedies. To him the Church indeed sings “mercy and judgment” (Psalm 101:1; LXX Psalm 100:1) (Genesis 1:26–27). He is kind to those who have done no wrong, and by a just judgment punishes those who, created good by God, sinned by their own will and rejected the help of mercy. This is the mercy and this the judgment sung by the Church of the catholics. In your church, however, nothing of the kind can resound, since it says that God, the Creator of evil people, without justice, judgment, or mercy, forms those whom he will punish, and punishes them because he himself formed them from Adam (Psalm 101:1;).

added_allusions.reason: Humanity is created as God’s image.

english: Let the dignity of the apostolic statement now be defended, lest it be thought that he meant about some people what you supposed about all. The apostle Paul, debating the objections of Jews who swelled with pride in the dignity of their ancestry and disdained believers from the nations being made equal to them, commends both God's justice and his grace. He argues that their generosity accounts both for the knowledge of the Law that first ennobled the Jews and for the preaching of Christ that afterward also admitted the nations. For there is one Creator of both peoples, who will judge the former through the Law, the latter without the Law, and the former in the Law (Romans 2:12; Romans 3:29–31). He is not the God of Jews alone but also of the nations (Romans 3:29), returning to each what belongs to that person without deceit or favoritism, that is, without partiality toward anyone. This is the sense of “favor” (Romans 2:6) in the definition of justice (compare Romans 2:6, 11).

Thus he rightly condemns those descended from Abraham when they live wickedly and drives them from his inheritance, just as he does Gentiles found acting similarly. Conversely, he rewards the good wills, true faith, and upright deeds of either people with eternal joys. The Teacher of the Nations therefore restrains Jewish pride and shows that the difference lies not in human seed but in conduct. They must recognize that unless they take care to be faithful, no privilege of circumcised ancestry will defend them. Jacob and Esau, after all, were conceived through one reception of seed and delivered through one act of giving birth, yet experienced very different outcomes because of the difference in what they deserved (compare Genesis 25:21–26; Romans 9:10–13) (Romans 2:11) (Genesis 25:21–26) (Romans 9:10–13) (Genesis 25:21–26; Romans 9:10–13).

english: For Esau, profane and sexually immoral, sold his birthright for a single meal. He sought the blessing he had despised and did not obtain it, although he begged for it with tears (Hebrews 12:16–17; Genesis 25:29–34; Genesis 27:34–38). Jacob, however, quiet and gentle, obedient to his parents' instructions and most eager for holy blessings, advanced so far that among the holy people God was called the God of Jacob as well as of Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 25:27; Genesis 27:8; Exodus 3:6; Matthew 22:32).

All examples therefore establish that by a just judgment God does not withhold his mercy from good minds in any nation, while allowing no nobility of ancestry to defend evil minds. The Jews should understand that they must not despise the nations' faith. Just as Israelite ancestry does not defend crimes, so Gentile descent is no obstacle to virtues. The apostle pursues all this in that debate. In some passages, however, to bow down the pride of the circumcised, he settles the issue on God's power alone under the name of grace (Genesis 25:29–34) (Genesis 27:34–38) (Genesis 25:27) (Genesis 27:8).

english: They boasted of observing ceremonies and sacrifices, and therefore supposed that other nations, consecrated by none of the Law's rites, neither could nor should suddenly be admitted to fellowship with them. He would tell them that even if the whole of righteousness had consisted in those observances, God would still have had power to make a change among the peoples, rejecting whom he wished and taking whom he wished. In answer to this meaning, a reply is made in the person of the Jews: nothing should now be demanded from the human will, since God “has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18). To this the apostle replies: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). He introduces the prophet Isaiah's testimony: “Does what is molded say to the one who molded it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’” (Isaiah 45:9; Romans 9:20). He adds in his own words: “Does the potter not have power over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:21).

The meaning is this: “Because I commended God's will and explained the authority of his grace, saying that he grants mercy to whomever he has mercy on, you, O Jew, raised a false accusation against me. You acted as though my commendation of divine will and power involved the destruction of divine justice. Because I said, ‘He does what he wills’, you argued that nothing should any longer be demanded of human will if God does everything according to his own will. Yet the dignity of the person concerned left no room for that objection. If I had said, ‘God does what he ought, according to the laws of his justice which judges each person's deserts’, you certainly would not have raised the objection you now raise. But because I said, ‘God does what he wills’, you thought I had stolen something from justice's dignity. Both statements, then, mean the same thing. When I say of God, ‘He does what he wills’, I say nothing other than, ‘He does what he ought’, because I know that he wills nothing other than what he ought. Where will is inseparably joined to fairness, whichever of them I name, I have indicated both.”

That pride wished to remain idle and cover its laziness with an appearance of necessity, so as to protest against the Gospel's reception of the nations. It therefore hears: “Even if matters were as you imagine, you should nevertheless petition God, not stir up a revolt.” With these words Paul checks the man's wickedness. Seizing upon ambiguous language, that man tried to attribute to divine necessity the difference in deserts that comes from the character of the will. He wanted to establish that one of two things must follow: either the nations do not enter into fellowship in the promise, or, if God is permitted to admit them, the tasks of free will are abolished.

But this did not suffice for the issue. Such a teacher could not commend God's authority while leaving his justice undefended. Most consistently, then, Paul adds that vessels made for dishonor and those made for honor receive this as the wages of their own will: “If God, wishing to show his wrath and make his power known with great patience in vessels of wrath completed for destruction, and to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy which he prepared for glory, whom he also called, namely us, not only from Jews but also from the nations” (Romans 9:22–24). Here he certainly clears up what the previous debate had concealed: God brings wrath only upon vessels completed for destruction, while glory is given to those prepared for it. By whom such vessels are prepared to receive the things we have named, the apostle's own words disclose: “In a great house there are not only gold and silver vessels but also wooden and earthenware ones, some for honor and some for dishonor. If, then, anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (2 Timothy 2:20–21).

See the task of free will: “If anyone cleanses himself” from association with cheap vessels, a name that denotes vices, “he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (2 Timothy 2:21). These vessels are therefore prepared for either wrath or glory through their own pursuits. God makes his power known in both cases, either by displaying severity toward the impious or by bestowing blessing on the faithful. It is therefore clear that this statement of the outstanding teacher has given no aid to Manichaean views; on the contrary, it has consistently armed us.

Consequently, it strongly opposed you too by saying that not everyone is formed for the condemnation into which you declare everyone goes. You habitually make the utterly absurd argument: “But those who are afterward freed are not formed for condemnation.” Yet not even the surface of the apostle's words can agree with you in that way. When you say, “Everyone is created for condemnation by the law of birth, but some, though very few, are freed from it through the mysteries”, you do not assert what he does. He proclaims not only that people are freed from among the condemned, but that not everyone is formed for condemnation: some are formed for dishonor, others for honor.

Just as it has become clear that the apostle said this about conduct, so it is apparent how desperately you lack the Law's testimonies. Against reason's thunderbolts you seek help from statements that disdain to assist you, indeed cannot assist you by their very nature.

These arguments concern the apostle's testimony. In Isaiah, however, from whom Paul took the statement itself, God is so far from deterring rational creatures from examining his judgment that he deigns to explain the reasoning of his dealings, lest he seem to have acted by power alone rather than justice. Through the same prophet he had said: “Cease acting perversely, learn to do good, help the oppressed; and come, argue with me, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:16–18) (Isaiah 29:16). Here likewise he announces to the Jewish people suffering in captivity that the time of redemption is approaching, when they will return to their own land. He discloses the reason both for their preceding distress and for their coming joy.

He says: “Let heaven above feast, and let the clouds scatter righteousness; let mercy arise from the earth, and let righteousness arise together with it. I am the Lord God who created you; making you better, I prepared you like a potter's clay. Will the plowman plow the earth all day? (Isaiah 28:24) Does the clay say to the potter, ‘What are you doing? You are not working; you have no hands’? Does what is molded say to the one who molded it, ‘Did you mold me wisely?’ (compare Isaiah 29:16) Or does someone say to a father, ‘What will you beget?’ and to a mother, ‘What will you give birth to?’ For thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, who made the things to come: ‘Question me about my sons and daughters, and give me instructions about the works of my hands. I made the earth and the human being upon it; with my own hand I established heaven; I commanded all the stars. I have raised up a king with righteousness, and all his ways are straight. He will build my city and bring back my people's captivity, not for a reward or for gifts,’ says the Lord of Hosts” (Isaiah 45:8–13, LXX-based wording).

english: In its historical meaning, then, this passage contains the following sense, as God speaks to the people: “I did not hand you over to captivity out of hatred, nor have I now released you from the bonds of Babylonian captivity through forgetfulness of judgment. As far as it lay with me, I was ready to cherish you with constant goodwill, but I owed it to my justice both to hand over sinners to their enemies and to restore and free those who had suffered. Someone skilled in farming does not always devote himself to one task, merely breaking the fields with the plowshare; he prepares the land in different ways for the fruitfulness he desires (Isaiah 28:24–29). So I too vary the turns of my dealings, so that by distress at one time and comfort at another I may fit your will for the fruits of righteousness.

To make you understand how fairly I deal with you, I could disregard your complaints on the strength of my power: just as something molded cannot say to its potter, ‘What have you done?’ (Isaiah 45:8–13), I could impose the weight of silence on you. Nevertheless, contrary to these examples, I invite you to question me about my sons and daughters, that is, yourselves and the works of my hands, and to learn that I have done everything justly and never anything cruelly.”

The farmer’s varied tasks explain the plowman quotation in the preceding section.

english: Both the prophet and the apostle therefore introduced the potter as an example to serve only as a comparison, not to indicate that human beings are as worthless in God's sight as clay is in potters' kiln and wheel. Having completed the explanation just given, we point out that according to the recent translation another meaning shines out in the same passage: “Drop dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one. Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise together with him. I, the Lord, created him. Woe to one who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among the earth's earthenware! Does the clay say to its potter, ‘What are you doing?’ and ‘Your work has no hands’?” (Isaiah 45:8–9).

Although historically these words describe King Cyrus, prophetically they describe the Savior's incarnation. Since he was to be born of the Virgin, the stubbornness of Jews and all unbelievers is challenged, so that they may not be enemies of trustworthy signs. For after saying, “Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise together with him”, he said: “I, the Lord, created him.”
translator_notes: The “recent translation” is distinguished from the LXX-based wording in section 138. Its “righteous one” and “Savior” support Julian’s explicitly prophetic reading alongside the historical reference to Cyrus.

english: The earth opens to bring forth a shoot before it receives seed through the cultivator's work. This is fulfilled in the Virgin's childbirth: through the gift of motherhood she preceded and excluded the function of a wife. Almighty God promises to do what was not customary. Foreseeing the multitude of unbelievers, he adds: “Woe to one who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among the earth's earthenware!” (Isaiah 45:9) (Luke 1:34–35). That is: “Woe to those who, despite God's promise, insist that a virgin could not become pregnant! Although every one of them is shaped in a mother's womb from seeds established by God, with God's power intervening, they obstinately insist that flesh could not have been fashioned from the Virgin's flesh without a man's service” (compare Luke 1:34–35).

“You stubborn people, when you think I could not do this and prescribe limits to me because of its difficulty, although you yourselves were plainly made by my hands, you are like clay that, while being worked by its potter, said to him, ‘You have no hands’, the very hands then shaping it into a vessel. So you who ask who gave the Virgin a son without a man's seed must recognize that it is the same one who made you from seed.”

But since Holy Scripture permits varied interpretation, and both explanations have harmonized in a devout and reverent way, let the first book now end. Let its ending nevertheless remind the reader to believe that God is the maker of newborn children, the protector of the innocent, the rewarder of catholics, and the condemner of Manichaeans.
